questions.q: What distinguishes a directed edge from an undirected edge in a graph?
options: A directed edge always carries a numerical traversal cost.
An undirected edge is symmetric, while a directed edge goes one way.
A directed edge connects a vertex back to itself exclusively.
questions.fact: An undirected edge connects two vertices symmetrically, while a directed edge goes in one direction.
why: Numerical costs define weighted graphs, not the direction of edges.
Undirected edges allow traversal both ways; directed edges permit one-way travel.
Connecting a vertex to itself is a self-loop, not a directed edge.

questions.q: What defines a cycle in a graph?
options: A path traversing every graph vertex exactly once.
A disconnected subgraph containing no undirected edges.
A path of edges that starts and ends at the same vertex.
questions.fact: A cycle is a path of edges that starts and ends at the same vertex.
why: Visiting every vertex once describes a Hamiltonian path, not a cycle.
A disconnected subgraph has no bearing on cyclical edge paths.
A cycle begins and ends at the identical vertex via edge traversal.

questions.q: How fast can you check whether an edge exists between two vertices in an adjacency matrix?
options: O(1) time by inspecting row u and column v.
O(V) time by iterating across all edges in the graph.
O(E) time by scanning through all connected neighbour lists.
questions.fact: In an adjacency matrix of size V × V, checking if an edge exists takes O(1) time.
why: Direct indexing into matrix cell [u][v] resolves in constant O(1) time.
No iteration is needed because the row and column give direct coordinates.
Scanning neighbour lists applies to adjacency lists, not an adjacency matrix.

questions.q: Why can an adjacency matrix be inefficient for storing large sparse graphs?
options: Checking adjacency between vertices takes linear O(V) lookup time.
It requires O(V²) memory regardless of how few edges exist.
It cannot represent graphs containing directed or weighted edges.
questions.fact: An adjacency matrix requires O(V²) memory, which can be wasteful for sparse graphs.
why: Matrix lookup is O(1), not O(V); memory is the primary inefficiency.
A V × V matrix allocates memory for every pair even with few edges.
Adjacency matrices easily represent directed and weighted graphs with numbers.

questions.q: Which data structure does breadth-first search use to explore neighbours level by level?
options: A call stack storing unvisited vertices via recursion.
A binary search tree ordering vertices by key.
A queue that processes vertices in FIFO order.
questions.fact: Breadth-first search (BFS) uses a queue to explore neighbours level by level in O(V + E) time.
why: A call stack is used by depth-first search, not breadth-first search.
A binary search tree does not manage traversal ordering in BFS.
A FIFO queue ensures vertices closer to the source are processed first.

questions.q: When is an undirected graph considered connected?
options: When there is a path between every pair of vertices.
When every vertex has an edge connecting to every other vertex.
When the total number of edges is strictly greater than V.
questions.fact: A graph is connected if there is a path between every pair of vertices.
why: A connected graph ensures every vertex can reach every other vertex.
Edges between all pairs defines a complete graph, not merely connected.
A connected graph needs only V − 1 edges, like in a tree.

questions.q: What defines a tree in graph theory?
options: Any directed graph where vertices have at most two incoming edges.
A connected undirected graph with no cycles and exactly V − 1 edges.
A complete graph containing cycles between all adjacent vertices.
questions.fact: A tree is a connected undirected graph with no cycles and exactly V − 1 edges.
why: Trees are undirected and acyclic; edge direction does not define general trees.
A tree connects all vertices without cycles using exactly V − 1 edges.
A complete graph contains many cycles, which violates the tree property.
